newsitem.title: UK: Hungary has worst heart disease record in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Hungary has worst heart disease record in Europe.

text.p: Heavy drinking and smoking and a fat-laden diet have helped push Hungary to the top of Europe's heart disease league, management consultancy Datamonitor said in a report on Monday.
Datamonitor said Hungary had one of the poorest life expectancy records in Europe, with average lifespans for men falling over the past 20 years to below 65.
By 1991 deaths from heart disease had risen sharply to 261 per 100,000 compared with 186 in 1971.
In contrast France, which has the best record in Europe, had a rate of just 61 deaths per 100,000, down from 105 in 1970.
In Britain the rate declined to 108 deaths per 100,000 from 202 in 1970. The European Union average dropped to 94 deaths from 147 in 1970.

The report said that in 1988 some 50 percent of Hungarians were found to be overweight, while the country also has the highest per capita consumption of tobacco in the world, 3.5 kilograms of tobacco a year compared with 1.5 in Britain.
"The trends in smoking and alcohol intake in Hungary infer that the incidence, prevalence and mortality of cardiovascular disease will increase in the future," Datamonitor said.
The report said drinking was a way of life in Hungary.

"It is not uncommon to start the day with a shot of vodka. As a consequence of such habits, deaths from liver cirrhosis ran at almost 5.8 percent of total deaths in 1995," and accounted for 7.9 percent of deaths among men.
Datamonitor said there had been a dramatic increase in the number of alcoholics in Hungary since 1980 because of "increased stress, due to lower salaries and longer working hours".
